If you're wondering...

How big can a chaos garden get?

Ecologically speaking, the answer is a given right away: the principles of a chaos garden have no upper limit. Diversity, closed loops, soil life allowed to do its work — a forest proves that the same principles still work at the scale of many hectares, and even better as the system grows bigger and older. Nature itself doesn't know a "too big for chaos." So the problem doesn't lie in the ecology. It lies in who has to walk around among those plants.

A fifty-square-meter chaos garden you can hold in your head. You know which corner stays damp after rain, where the lettuce got sick last year, which two plants happened to do well next to each other. That knowledge is intuitive and grows naturally with the time you spend in the garden. Make that same garden ten times bigger, and that intuition can no longer keep up — you simply can't keep following every square meter with the same attention. What's unplanned, lively chaos at small scale quickly becomes, at large scale, simply this: unmanaged.

That's where the real limit pinches: not how big a system is allowed to be ecologically, but how much one person — or a pair of hands — can keep actively observing, adjusting, and harvesting. Sooner or later you reach a point where growth forces a choice. Either you expand the labor: more hands, shared work, a garden that's no longer one person's but a group's. Or you shift part of the system toward structures that can carry more of themselves — fewer annual crops that need yearly attention, more permanent planting that, as in a food forest, can largely carry on without you after the start-up years. Or, past a certain size, you bring machines into play, and the shape shifts toward rows and strips as in agroforestry — not because chaos stops working there, but because a tractor needs to be able to read it.

So a chaos garden isn't limited by how big nature can still be — that can always be bigger. It's limited by how much you, with the time and attention you have, can still personally keep knowing. That's not a shortcoming of the principle, it's simply the limit of one pair of eyes and hands. If your garden grows past that limit, the question grows with it: who or what takes over that attention from you.

Chaos has no upper limit — your attention does. A chaos garden grows as long as you still know it; past that point, something else has to take over: more hands, more self-sufficiency from the plants themselves, or more structure.
